question: Measuring water quality in the EU requires intensive monitoring at measuring points – not least to establish nitrate concentrations in watercourses so as to meet the objectives of the Nitrates Directive. However, each Member State has its own specific measurement method and organises its network of measuring points differently.

Some Member States measure only at large watercourses, while others operate on a much more granular basis and also have measuring points on all smaller watercourses. This potentially creates a distortion, with more rigorous measurement in some Member States producing a more negative outcome by comparison with others, while not automatically reflecting reality correctly. 1.
Does the Commission have details of the comparability of the organisational set-up for measuring points in the Member States?
If not: does the Commission propose to look into the organisational set-up for water quality measuring points so as to ensure a level playing field in the EU?
Can Member States modify their monitoring systems based on measuring points so as, for instance, to make them more granular or scale them back so that they cover only large watercourses?
answer: Monitoring programmes under the Water Framework Directive (1) (WFD), and its two so-called daughter Directives (2), (3), are intended to determine the condition of surface and groundwaters, detect changes and inform the identification of measures to ensure that drinking water sources are protected and good status is achieved, meaning the good chemical and ecological status of surface waters and the good chemical and quantitative status of groundwaters.

Under the Nitrates Directive (4) (ND) monitoring is required to identify the areas where water is polluted with nitrates from agriculture and to assess the effectiveness of the measures in place to reduce such pollution.

While Member States have the flexibility to establish their monitoring networks and programmes to adapt to local conditions and pressures, it is essential to ensure a level playing field across the EU. The directives, e.g.

, Annex V to the WFD, include specific requirements, and the location of monitoring points must provide a comprehensive and representative overview of the water body status, ensuring a standardised approach across all Member States. Monitoring guidance has been published in relation to the WFD (5).

The Commission assesses the robustness of national monitoring and classification systems as part of its assessment of the River Basin Management Plans (RBMPs) under the WFD. Bilateral exchanges were held with Member States to improve monitoring across the EU following the assessment of the second RBMPs.

If the assessment of the third RBMPs shows that little or no progress has been made, the Commission may take further action. The current evaluation (6) of the ND will also consider its alignment with the WFD in terms of monitoring and reporting requirements.
